indicators.Soil type: NSW DPIRD: 'Trees can grow on all soil types, though they grow best on well-drained, sandier soils along dry creek beds.' HerbiGuide: 'On many well drained soils. More abundant on red brown earths, loamy and clay soils. Establishes rapidly on dry creek beds.' Weeds Australia: grows in 'a huge variety of climates, habitats, soil types'. Practical reading: not a soil-type indicator, but strongest on well-drained, often sandy/alluvial creek-line soils.
indicators.Moisture: NSW DPIRD: 'African boxthorn is drought tolerant' and grows best on well-drained soils 'along dry creek beds'. HerbiGuide: 'Establishes rapidly on dry creek beds'; occurs in temperate, Mediterranean, sub-humid and semi-arid subtropical regions. Indicates dry, well-drained, drought-prone sites (creek lines, rangelands) rather than moist or waterlogged ground.
indicators.Disturbance: Weeds Australia: 'It grows on waste-land, creek-beds, along waterways, fence-lines, roadsides, sandy and coastal areas, in woodlands, in rangelands and uncultivated pastures.' NSW DPIRD lists woodlands, rangelands and uncultivated pastures, open coastal areas, roadsides and waterways. Suggests heavily grazed/broken country and waste areas rather than a strict disturbance indicator.
indicators.General indicators: Temperate, subtropical and semi-arid Australia; agricultural and native vegetation, waste-land, creek-beds, along waterways, fence-lines, roadsides, sandy and coastal areas, woodlands, rangelands and uncultivated pastures (Weeds Australia; NSW DPIRD). Common near the sea in SA (HerbiGuide). A Weed of National Significance. Note: Weeds Australia states the NATIVE Lycium australe - not L. ferocissimum - is the Lycium found on subsaline soils.

indicators.Moisture: Indicates wet, poorly drained and periodically inundated ground as well as open water. NSW WeedWise: 'Alligator weed will grow in ponded and flowing waterways, on the banks of waterways, on floodplains and poorly drained land, and less commonly in drier situations above flood level', and it 'can easily tolerate dry periods'. Weeds Australia: 'Ideal terrestrial habitats include places that are regularly inundated or that have high rainfall or irrigation.' HerbiGuide adds it 'is rooted in the bottom mud and cannot survive in water exceeding 2500 mm in depth'.
indicators.Fertility: Indicates nutrient-rich (eutrophic) fresh water and enriched wet soils. Weeds Australia: it 'grows in creeks, rivers, ponds and drainage channels and thrives in nutrient-rich fresh water'. NSW WeedWise's control guidance for the aquatic situation recommends reducing nutrient levels in waterways by managing erosion on cultivated land, controlling stock access and diverting effluent.
indicators.Salinity: Tolerant of brackish conditions, so its presence does NOT indicate fresh water only. NSW WeedWise: 'Infestations have been found growing in saline conditions (flowing water with 30% of the salinity of seawater), and on beaches above the high tide zone.' Weeds Australia: 'It can also tolerate 10% sea-strength salinity or up to 30% salinity in flowing brackish water, e.g. adjacent to or in mangrove and beach areas in coastal regions.' HerbiGuide gives the same 10%/30% figures.
indicators.Soil type: Not texture-specific. NSW WeedWise: 'Alligator weed will grow in a range of soils and substrates from sand to heavy clay, and can easily tolerate dry periods.' Roots are 'relatively fine and short in water but become thicker, starchy and rhizome-like in soil, able to penetrate to depths of over 50 cm' with roots and stems found more than 1 m below the surface.
indicators.Disturbance: Indicates disturbed, nutrient-enriched and modified waterways and floodplains rather than intact vegetation. NSW WeedWise: it 'disrupts the aquatic environment by blanketing the surface', 'competes with and displaces native flora along river and creek banks and in wetlands', and 'the most significant spread between catchments in NSW has been through the commercial and recreational activities of people'. HerbiGuide notes 'The main nuisance results from the restriction of water flow and the acceleration of siltation', i.e. it is associated with silted, slow-flowing systems.
indicators.General indicators: Aquatic and terrestrial in cool to warm temperate, subtropical and tropical Australia: creeks, rivers, ponds, dams, drainage channels, wetlands, floodplains, seasonally flooded agricultural and grazing land and irrigation systems, plus beaches above the high tide zone in coastal regions. In NSW the main infestations are in the Lower Hunter, the Sydney basin, the Hawkesbury-Nepean and Barren Box Swamp near Griffith.

indicators.General indicators: THE iconic Australian indicator of extremely low-P soils. Banksia leaf P concentrations are an order of magnitude lower than crop plants.; Many species (e.g., B. attenuata) restricted to deep Bassendean sands — presence indicates ancient, deeply leached sand soils.; Banksia re-mobilises P from senescing leaves to levels (27 µg P/g DM) lower than any other plant species recorded — this extreme adaptation only makes sense on extremely P-poor soils.; Strongest indicator of ancient, unglaciated, deeply weathered soils — the SW Australian landscape where Banksia dominates has been weathering for 250+ million years.; Typically non-mycorrhizal — cluster roots replace mycorrhizal function; this strategy only works where P is extremely limiting.; Australia-wide (173 species) but centre of diversity in SW Western Australia (kwongan).

indicators.Soil pH: Landscape SA (Northern and Yorke): bridal creeper 'can grow in most soils ... It is particularly vigorous in alkaline sandy soils and also thrives in areas high in nutrients such as creeks and drainage lines.' This is the only Australian pH statement found for this species; no numeric pH range was given.
indicators.Soil type: NSW DPIRD: 'Bridal creeper tolerates a wide range of soil types though it prefers light sand or loams.' HerbiGuide: 'Found on sand, sandy loam, sandy limestone, sandy clay soils, limestone formations, sandy coastal dunes and most other soils. Rare on heavy grey clay and laterite soils.' Landscape SA: 'can grow in most soils'.
indicators.Moisture: NSW DPIRD: 'It thrives in well drained, moist, fertile soils'; it 'requires at least 350 mm of rain per year' and 'once the tubers develop it can tolerate droughts'. Landscape SA: 'thrives in areas high in nutrients such as creeks and drainage lines'; 'foliage dies off in summer due to lack of water, but tuber reserves enable bridal creeper to survive summer drought'. Weeds Australia: 'well-drained' soils.
indicators.Fertility: NSW DPIRD: 'It thrives in well drained, moist, fertile soils.' Landscape SA: 'thrives in areas high in nutrients such as creeks and drainage lines'. Weeds Australia: 'preferring fertile, well-drained soils of light texture'.
indicators.Disturbance: Mixed signal - do not treat as a reliable disturbance indicator. NSW DPIRD records it in 'a wide range of disturbed sites including roadsides and drains', but Landscape SA states 'unlike many other weeds, bridal creeper is capable of colonising undisturbed ecosystems'. NSW DPIRD also notes 'Plants mostly grow in part or full shade'.
indicators.General indicators: Subtropical to cool/warm temperate southern Australia; a Weed of National Significance in woodlands and along roadsides. NSW DPIRD: orchards but not usually cropping or grazing land; also roadsides and drains, sand dunes and coastal heath, mallee shrubland, eucalypt and banksia woodlands and forests, edges of waterways and swamps, littoral rainforest. Landscape SA: most common closer to the coast, invading woodlands and open coastal vegetation; creeks and drainage lines. HerbiGuide adds: found along creeks, Eucalyptus/Banksia woodlands, coastal heath, wet and dry sclerophyll forest, riparian vegetation.

indicators.Moisture: Germination is moisture-limited. GRDC integrated weed management manual: 'Moisture is the main requirement for brome grass germination, as seed will germinate over a wide range of temperatures', with the first flush after the opening autumn rains being the most prominent. HerbiGuide records it as 'Relatively drought tolerant'; Lucid/Weeds of Australia notes it grows 'in damp sites near creeks and wetlands' as well as drier sites.
indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: 'It is a common pasture plant on sandier soil types', and its roots 'occur mainly in the top 10 cm of soil'. The GRDC manual notes persistence 'could be prolonged on non-wetting soils, with high levels of seedbank carryover (30%) from one season to the next'.
indicators.Disturbance: Indicates cultivated and disturbed ground, and its germination is stimulated by tillage. HerbiGuide: 'Germination is often stimulated by cultivation that buries the seed'; 'After ripening period is less under stubble than on bare soil'. The GRDC manual: 'Seeds do not germinate until shallow burial by the sowing operation, prompting a larger in-crop flush of brome grasses', and 'seed germination resumes upon release from innate dormancy and placement in complete darkness caused by tillage or sowing operations'; establishment 'is more rapid and uniform when emerging from under wheat stubble than on bare soil and higher if seed is mixed with the soil by shallow cultivation'. Lucid/Weeds of Australia calls it 'a common weed of pastures, crops and disturbed sites'.
indicators.General indicators: Widely naturalised in southern Australia (south-eastern Queensland, throughout NSW and Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania, larger parts of South Australia, southern Northern Territory and southern and western WA); a common weed of pastures, crops and disturbed sites, and also growing in native grasslands, woodlands, coastal sites, offshore islands and damp sites near creeks and wetlands; an environmental weed in Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia and one of the top ten environmental weeds of coastal environs in the Gascoyne region of WA.

indicators.Soil type: AWRI's soil-indicator entry states caltrop 'occurs on a wide range of soils but is more abundant on sandy soils'. Weeds Australia (quoting Parsons & Cuthbertson 1992) places it 'mostly in open waste places ... particularly in districts with high summer temperatures and dry sandy soils where there is little competition'. HerbiGuide: 'Occurs on a wide range of soils. More abundant on sandy soils.'
indicators.Moisture: AWRI: caltrop 'is drought tolerant but is intolerant to waterlogging'. The Victorian Weed Risk Assessment (VRO, archived) records 'its extensive root system allows it to survive droughts' and that 'seeds germinate after late spring and summer rains'. Net reading: dry, well-drained, summer-moist sites; not waterlogged ground.
indicators.Fertility: AWRI lists caltrop as 'an indicator of low calcium, very low potassium and organic matter, high phosphorus, magnesium, iron, and aluminium' - i.e. an indicator of nutrient imbalance rather than of generally high fertility. The page gives no primary citation for this indicator list (its linked resource is HerbiGuide), so treat as medium confidence.
indicators.Organic matter: AWRI lists caltrop as an indicator of 'very low ... organic matter' in the soil.
indicators.Disturbance: SA PIRSA: 'Caltrop is favoured by bare ground, and does not compete effectively with other plants. Management to maintain a dense ground cover significantly reduces germination.' AWRI quotes a Henschke Wines case study: caltrop 'hates competition', found isolated to 'bare patches of soil on headlands' and spread on vehicle tyres.
indicators.General indicators: Open waste places, roadsides, overgrazed pastures, stock yards and neglected areas; also crops and orchards/vineyards; districts with high summer temperatures and little competition (Weeds Australia, quoting Parsons & Cuthbertson 1992). PIRSA lists habitat simply as 'gardens, pastures'. HerbiGuide lists 'pastures, crops, vineyards, orchards, cotton, horticulture, roadsides, stockyards, bushland, parks, stock routes and disturbed areas'.

indicators.General indicators: THE premier indicator of severely phosphorus-impoverished soils. Hakea species occur on some of the most P-impoverished soils in the world (southwest Australia).; Presence of Hakea indicates ancient, deeply weathered, nutrient-depleted landscapes — southwest Australia has not been glaciated or inundated for 250+ million years.; The development of proteoid (cluster) roots is a direct response to low P — cluster roots are suppressed when P is adequate, making their presence on roots a direct indicator of P deficiency.; Many Hakea species are P-sensitive — they suffer toxicity at moderate P levels that would be normal for crop plants. This is itself an indicator: if Hakea are healthy, P is extremely low.; Typically non-mycorrhizal (unlike most plants on low-P soils) — they have evolved cluster roots instead of mycorrhizal associations.; Southwest Australia (centre of diversity — ~70% of 150 species endemic to SWAFR); also eastern Australia.

indicators.Moisture: A winter-growing annual of temperate southern Australia that 'prefers hot dry summers and mild wet winters' (HerbiGuide). The GRDC integrated weed management manual describes it as 'a winter fallow and crop weed due to its soil moisture preference and effect on crop yield loss', well adapted to 'the winter rainfall regions of southern Australia, which are characterised by hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters', with 'the majority of shallowly buried seed will germinate in autumn and early winter, when undisturbed conditions favour seedling survival' and peak germination (80% of seeds) 'at the break of season after the first two falls of rain that exceed 20 mm'.
indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: 'Prefers heavy soils. Common on sandy, loamy red and heavy grey clays.' Also notes emergence behaviour differs by texture - 'On heavy soils the maximum emergence occurs on undisturbed areas whereas in light soils a shallow cultivation increases emergence substantially.' The GRDC integrated weed management manual adds that it 'is well adapted to most soil types in the winter rainfall regions of southern Australia'.
indicators.Disturbance: An indicator of cultivated, disturbed and fallow land rather than intact vegetation. HerbiGuide lists it as a 'Weed of rotation crops, perennial crops, fallows, gardens, lawns and disturbed areas', and notes that on non-wetting soils germination conditions may not occur, causing seed carry-over, and that 'there may be greater Annual Ryegrass seed carry over into the following season in undisturbed (zero tillage) areas'. Lucid/Weeds of Australia records it as a widespread weed of crops that 'also invades natural vegetation' and is an environmental weed in Victoria and Western Australia.
indicators.General indicators: Widely naturalised in southern, central and eastern Australia and most widespread in NSW, the ACT, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and south-western WA; a major weed of winter crops, pastures, fallows, gardens, lawns and disturbed areas, and also an environmental weed invading natural vegetation in Victoria and Western Australia.

indicators.General indicators: Premier indicator of tropical floodplain wetland degradation in northern Australia — forms dense monospecific thickets that replace all native vegetation.; Invasion pattern follows floodplains and seasonally inundated wetlands; spread primarily by floodwater seed dispersal.; "Highest densities of outbreaks in wetland margins disturbed by feral animals" — indicator of combined feral animal + weed impact on wetlands.; Prefers "wetland habitats with a relatively long period of inundation but where trees were absent" — indicator of treeless floodplain vulnerability.; Seeds remain viable for 22+ years — indicates persistent weed seedbank in wetland soils.; Blocks access to water for stock; prevents harvesting of bush foods by Indigenous people.; Currently ~85,000–140,000 ha in NT (Adelaide, Finniss, Reynolds, Mary, Daly, East Alligator, South Alligator, Victoria, Phelp River systems). One outbreak near Proserpine, QLD (2001).

indicators.Structure: Strongest indicator of heavy grey cracking clay soils (vertisols) in northern Australia. These soils store subsoil moisture critical for summer-growing Mitchell grass.
indicators.General indicators: Dominance of Mitchell grass indicates good pasture condition; decline and replacement by annual grasses and weeds indicates overgrazing.; Only palatable when very young — heavy grazing reduces/eliminates Mitchell grass. However, it responds well after grazing rest with summer rainfall.; 250–550 mm annual rainfall; summer-dominant rainfall pattern.; Extensive grasslands across QLD, northern NSW, NT, and northern WA.

indicators.Soil pH: Weeds Australia states serrated tussock 'will grow in acid soils', so its presence is compatible with acidic soils; no alkaline limit is given. NSW WeedWise gives no pH figure and no Australian source consulted stated a numeric pH range.
indicators.Moisture: Occupies both dry and moist ground - Weeds Australia places it 'on low-fertility and dry soils' as well as on 'fertile moist flats' - and it is drought tolerant, with drought-caused bare ground favouring it. Its distribution is 'limited by salinity and / or water-logging', so its presence indicates ground that is not waterlogged.
indicators.Fertility: Indicates low soil fertility / nutrient-poor soil. NSW WeedWise states 'Sandy, nutrient poor soils are at most risk' of invasion, and Weeds Australia lists 'low-fertility and dry soils' among the situations it grows on (while noting it also grows on 'rich to poor degraded soils').
indicators.Salinity: Indicates non-saline soil. NSW WeedWise lists 'saline soils or salty areas' among the situations serrated tussock 'does not grow well in', and Weeds Australia states its distribution 'is limited by salinity'.
indicators.Soil type: Tolerates 'shallow soil if it is not in competition with other plants' and grows on 'soils derived from basalt, granite, shale, slate and sandstone' (NSW WeedWise). Weeds Australia describes it as 'adapted to a wide range of climates and soil types', growing 'from steep, rocky and timbered areas, on low-fertility and dry soils, to fertile moist flats'. No single texture preference is stated by either source.
indicators.Disturbance: A strong bare-ground/disturbance indicator. NSW WeedWise: 'Serrated tussock colonises bare areas. Drought causing bare ground favours serrated tussock.' Weeds Australia: it 'quickly colonises bare ground and disturbed areas such as roadsides, overgrazed pastures or cultivated situations', and its seedlings are 'usually out-competed by other plants, but become competitive under conditions of drought or overstocking when more favourable pasture species are consumed by stock'.
indicators.General indicators: Temperate south-eastern Australia (far north-eastern NSW south to Victoria and eastern Tasmania), on pastures, native grasslands, open scrub and woodland, roadsides, overgrazed pastures and cultivated situations; cool temperate areas with 450-1000 mm annual rainfall, on all terrain and aspects, from steep rocky timbered country to fertile moist flats; also invades urban roadsides, railways, power-line easements and reserves.

indicators.Fertility: NSW DPI Primefact 923 (repeated on NSW WeedWise): 'It is usually found on soils of moderate to high fertility in areas with an annual rainfall of 500-900 mm.'
indicators.Moisture: NSW DPI: annual rainfall 500-900 mm, and seed 'can germinate at any time of the year provided there is moisture available'. Weeds Australia (citing DPI NSW 2019): found 'on well-drained sites'. HerbiGuide: 'Prefers moist, highly fertile, well drained sites.' Indicates moist but well-drained, cooler high-rainfall country (it requires vernalisation/chilling).
indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: nodding thistle 'grows on a wide range of soil types'; Weeds Australia places it in open situations such as pasture, road edges and grasslands in temperate Australia.
indicators.Disturbance: NSW DPI: 'the development of bare patches, particularly during peak germination time, provides an ideal habitat for nodding thistle establishment'; it 'is intolerant of competition for light, particularly during the germination stage'. Weeds Australia: 'The presence of disturbed sites in pastures and native grasslands at the end of summer favours its establishment.'
indicators.Soil pH: HerbiGuide states nodding thistle 'prefers dry alkaline soils in its native range'. This is explicitly about its native (European) range and is NOT evidence that it indicates alkaline soils in Australia - flagged as low confidence for AU use, and no Australian source stating a pH preference was found.
indicators.General indicators: Cool temperate Australia only, because it requires vernalisation (chilling) to flower - about one million hectares of the NSW tablelands plus small areas in the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania. An aggressive competitor of pastures; occurs in dense patches, not readily grazed; open situations such as pasture, road edges and grasslands, in areas of 500-900 mm annual rainfall (NSW DPI; Weeds Australia).

indicators.General indicators: THE premier Australian indicator species for groundwater depth. Critical thresholds identified at 12.1–22.6 m — beyond this, canopy condition declines abruptly.; In upper Murray (fresh groundwater <15 mS/cm²), dieback increases with increasing depth. In lower Murray (saline >30 mS/cm²), condition improves with depth as trees avoid saline groundwater.; Indicator of floodplain health and hydrological connectivity. Requires periodic flooding for recruitment.; Trees on shallow groundwater (<2–3 m) have greater growth rates and are less reactive to drought.; 70% of Victorian Murray River floodplain forest dying back — condition directly tied to groundwater access.; Most widespread eucalypt on mainland Australia; all states except TAS.

indicators.Moisture: A free-floating aquatic fern - an indicator of standing or slow-moving fresh water, not of soil. NSW WeedWise: 'It grows best in warm fresh water that is still or slow-flowing and has high nutrient levels.' Weeds Australia: 'usually found in still or slow-moving water bodies with high nutrient levels normally favouring warmer climates, but is found growing in cooler temperate southern Australia', with growth limited or absent under 10 degrees C.
indicators.Fertility: Indicates high nutrient (eutrophic) water. NSW WeedWise: it grows best in water with 'high nutrient levels', and fronds are 'yellowish in low nutrient water'; recommended control includes reducing nutrient levels by managing erosion on cultivated land, controlling stock access to banks and waterways and diverting effluent. Weeds Australia: 'Salvinia grows faster and produces more growth the higher the nutrient levels in a water body. Reducing the growth and biomass of Salvina [sic] involves reducing nutrient levels in waterways.'
indicators.Disturbance: HerbiGuide describes it as a 'Very serious weed of waterways, reservoirs, streams and rice fields', and NSW WeedWise notes plants spread by water flows especially floods and wind and that rain 'can also stimulate growth by washing nutrients into the water' - i.e. it responds to nutrient inputs from disturbed/cultivated catchments rather than to soil disturbance.
indicators.General indicators: Still or slow-moving fresh water bodies - waterways, reservoirs, streams, dams, drains and rice fields - in tropical and subtropical climates, with growth best between 20 and 30 degrees C and limited or absent under 10 degrees C, but able to persist in cooler temperate southern Australia; a Weed of National Significance and one of Australia's worst aquatic weeds.

indicators.Moisture: NSW WeedWise: 'Gorse grows across a wide range of rainfall and soil conditions' and 'grows in full sun to moderate shade'. indicators.Fertility: Associated with fertile soils: HerbiGuide states gorse is most abundant on 'fertile acidic soils'. It is also a nitrogen-fixing legume, so it can colonise and then enrich low-nitrogen sites rather than indicating high soil nitrogen.
indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: 'Grows well on most soils from light sands to heavy clays' - i.e. a wide soil-texture tolerance rather than a texture indicator.
indicators.Disturbance: Indicates disturbed, neglected and unimproved land. NSW WeedWise lists 'disturbed sites such as roadsides, along railway lines, in quarries and mine sites', and notes 'significant germination and survival events also occur after fire or soil disturbance'. Weeds Australia describes it as 'an invasive weed of unimproved grazing land, neglected sites, roadsides and forest margins'. HerbiGuide describes gorse as 'a primary coloniser'.
indicators.General indicators: Cool to warm temperate southern Australia with 450-2400 mm rainfall; a major agricultural weed in Tasmania and parts of Victoria, invading unimproved, semi-improved and improved pastures, neglected cropping land, roadsides, railway lines, quarries, mine sites, forest margins, riparian zones, heathland, lowland grassland, grassy woodland and dry and damp sclerophyll forest. In NSW the largest infestations are on the Southern and Central Tablelands.

indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: 'More abundant on granite derived soils, loams, black earths, volcanic, alluvial and fertile soils.' Weeds Australia: 'fertile soils of alluvial or volcanic origin, and on some sandy or sandy loam soils'.

HerbiGuide: 'More abundant in wetter areas'; climate described as temperate/Mediterranean/sub-humid warm temperate. Landscape SA: germination follows autumn rain and the plant 'grows rapidly in spring'.
indicators.Disturbance: Landscape SA: variegated thistle 'needs bare or disturbed ground to germinate'. Weeds Australia: 'common on sheep and cattle camps in pastures'; also 'cultivated land, roadsides, stockyards, and disturbed neglected areas and disturbed areas in woodlands and open forests'. Stock camps imply nutrient-enriched, bare, pugged ground.
indicators.General indicators: Well-watered temperate regions of southern Australia; pasture (especially sheep and cattle camps), cultivated land, roadsides, stockyards, disturbed neglected areas, and disturbed areas in woodlands and open forests (Weeds Australia, quoting Parsons & Cuthbertson 1992). In SA it is a competitive pasture weed, worst in higher-rainfall agricultural districts (Landscape SA).

indicators.Soil pH: HerbiGuide states wild oat 'grows on a wide range of soil acidities from pH 4.5-9' - i.e. it is not a useful pH indicator, spanning strongly acidic to alkaline soils.
indicators.Moisture: Germination is moisture-driven: HerbiGuide records that it 'germinates from autumn to spring with a flush in autumn and is dependent on moisture, soil disturbance, temperature and short term dormancy', with little germination above 27 degrees C. Lucid/Weeds of Australia notes it 'is a common weed of wetlands in the southern parts of Western Australia'.
indicators.Soil type: HerbiGuide: 'Found on most soil types, but prefers the heavy grey clays and in particular the self mulching soils.' The GRDC integrated weed management manual states that 'soil type doesn't greatly influence the weed's distribution although wild oats can emerge from a greater depth in lighter textured soils' - i.e. heavy clays are preferred but lighter textured soils allow deeper emergence.
indicators.Disturbance: Indicates cultivation and disturbed ground. HerbiGuide lists its habitat as 'Roadsides, cultivated crops and disturbed areas' and notes seed is returned to the surface by tillage; Lucid/Weeds of Australia describes it as 'a common weed of roadsides, railway lines, disturbed sites, waste areas, parks, gardens and disturbed and undisturbed natural habitats (e.g. grasslands, shrublands, open woodlands and along waterways)'.
indicators.General indicators: Very widely naturalised in southern and eastern Australia (throughout NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, the ACT, southern South Australia and south-western/western WA, plus semi-arid and sub-tropical regions); a major weed of cereal crops and a common weed of roadsides, railway lines, disturbed sites, waste areas, parks, gardens, grasslands, shrublands, open woodlands and waterways, and an environmental weed in NSW, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia.
